newsitem.title: USA: Fed policy factors in CPI bias - Atl Fed economist.
newsitem.headline: Fed policy factors in CPI bias - Atl Fed economist.

text.p: Possible overstatement of inflation in the Consumer Price Index and measurement errors in other indicators are a concern for Federal Reserve policymakers when they set official interest rates, Robert Eisenbeis, Director of Research at the Atlanta Fed, said.
"When inflation is at a low level, we are concerned about measurement errors," Eisenbeis pointed out, calling the "bias in the CPI critical" for Fed policy.
"We are not afraid of growth at all. If we were, we would have taken action long time ago," he added.

"If your (policy) target is a number like inflation, you must be confident you're capturing the facts," Eisenbeis, who took the helm of the Atlanta Fed's research department this summer, told Reuters in interviews on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Eisenbeis stressed the Fed is watchful "about not giving up ground when it comes to progress against inflation" when the U.S. economy enjoys solid growth. He said the Fed is also looking at "what is the appropriate index" for measuring inflation.
Fed chairman Alan Greenspan has said CPI may overstate inflation by as much as one percentage point.
"Should it be some number like the CPI or some number like the (Gross Domestic Product) deflator which is a broader measure of price performance," Eisenbeis asked.
Core CPI rose at a 2.7-percent pace year-over-year in July. The second-quarter GDP price deflator inched up by a more modest 2.2 percent.
Regarding wage gains, Eisenbeis the Fed would regard wages rising with productivity gains as non-inflationary.
"Productivity growth, that's another place where we don't have a good understanding of measurement," Eisenbeis said.

"This kind of wage increases is not only great but does not trigger any policy issue. If wages go up because of increased productivity, that's not inflationary," Eisenbeis said, noting that higher wages historically have followed productivity gains.
But Eisenbeis also stressed "the jury is still out" on such issues at the Fed, largely because productivity is difficult to measure in the services sector.
Eisenbeis said a number of developments such as growing use of technology and changes in employee benefits hinted at measurement errors.
"We know what is happening with productivity in manufacturing. It's going up. It's hard for me to believe the CPI has captured changes in an industry like architecture."
Eisenbeis noted that computer models now allow architects and engineers to design buildings and structures without spending lenghty -- and costly -- hours at the drawing board.
He added that changes in financial markets have altered the way monetary policy affects the economy.

"In the old days, if you raised interest rates, this would chop down housing. You identified a sector that bears the brunt of monetary changes," Eisenbeis noted. "We are now dealing with a system whose channels are not so direct."
Eisenbeis said shopping for mortgage rates through new means such at the Internet gives buyers access to the best deals regardless of their location.
Eisenbeis also noted an array of private and corporate loans are now pegged to the Treasury yield curve rather than to benchmark rates such as the discount rate.

"It's a better situation because, while this may increase the lag effect on how monetary policy works, it has a fairer effect in the sense policy changes are channeled through all the economy," Eisenbeis said. He said policy makers are sometimes baffled by market reactions to single indicators.
Eisenbeis, who, in the past, served as a senior economist at the Fed Board, was in Boston for the annual conference of the National Association of Business Economists.
